Polyphony. The texture of simultaneous independent melodic lines, each with its own rhythmic and pitch identity, interweaving to create harmony. It stands opposite to monophony, which is a single line, and homophony, where chords support a melody, and it is the foundation of much Western classical music, from medieval organum through Bach and beyond.

For polyphonic texture to work, each voice needs to be relatively independent and interesting on its own. If all the voices move together in the same rhythm, the result is homophonic, not polyphonic. Counterpoint is the disciplined art of writing polyphony according to historical rules, while free polyphony loosens those rules for contemporary or expressive freedom.

Medieval organum was one of the earliest polyphonic forms, pairing a chant with an added voice. Renaissance motets expanded the technique to four or six voices. Fugue, canon, and round are all polyphonic forms, as are many passages in symphonies—particularly the development section of a sonata—and in chamber music.

The Renaissance in the sixteenth century and the Baroque era from the seventeenth into the early eighteenth century both prioritized polyphony. Classical and Romantic composers shifted emphasis to homophony but used polyphony selectively for contrast and depth. Understanding counterpoint, the formal study of how to write polyphonic lines properly, remains essential to anyone studying polyphony.
